subject: chem
title: Energetics
subtitle: Enthalpy changes, Hess's law and bond energies.
concept: Enthalpy change (ΔH) measures heat energy exchanged at constant pressure. Exothermic reactions release heat (ΔH < 0); endothermic absorb it (ΔH > 0).
Hess's law: total enthalpy change is independent of route taken — only depends on initial and final states.
Bond enthalpy calculations estimate ΔH from energy needed to break bonds (endothermic) minus energy released forming bonds (exothermic).

notes.heading: Enthalpy Change and Standard Conditions
items: Enthalpy change (ΔH) is the heat energy exchanged at constant pressure. Exothermic reactions release heat (ΔH < 0); endothermic reactions absorb it (ΔH > 0).
Standard conditions: 298 K (25 °C) and 100 kPa, with all substances in their standard states. Standard enthalpy changes carry the symbol ΔH⊖.
Standard enthalpy of formation (ΔHf⊖): enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound forms from its elements in standard states. By convention, ΔHf⊖ of any element in its standard state = 0.
Standard enthalpy of combustion (ΔHc⊖): enthalpy change when 1 mol burns completely in O₂ under standard conditions.
Standard enthalpy of neutralisation (ΔHneut⊖): enthalpy change when 1 mol of water forms from H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). For strong acid + strong base ≈ −57 kJ mol⁻¹.

notes.heading: Hess's Law
items: Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken — it depends only on the initial and final states (a consequence of conservation of energy).
Combustion cycle: ΔH(reaction) = ΣΔHc⊖(reactants) − ΣΔHc⊖(products) — note the reversed sign compared to the formation version.
Always draw the Hess cycle with clear arrows before doing arithmetic.

notes.heading: Calorimetry
items: q = mcΔT, where m = mass of solution in grams, c = specific heat capacity of water (4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹), ΔT = temperature change in °C (or K — the difference is identical).
ΔH = −q / n  (negative sign: if the solution warms, the reaction is exothermic — energy was released TO the solution).
Key sources of error: heat loss to surroundings and calorimeter; incomplete combustion; assuming density of solution = 1 g cm⁻³.

notes.heading: Bond Enthalpies
items: ΔH = Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds broken) − Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds formed). Breaking bonds is endothermic (+); forming bonds is exothermic (−).
Mean bond enthalpies are averages over many molecules — they give approximate (not exact) ΔH values. Hess's law cycles using ΔHf⊖ or ΔHc⊖ data give exact values.
Always draw the full displayed structural formula before counting bonds.

definitions.body: Reaction where energy is released to the surroundings; ΔH is negative.
Enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its constituent elements in their standard states at 298 K.
The total enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided initial and final conditions are the same.
The average energy required to break one mole of a given bond in the gaseous phase, averaged over many different compounds.

workedExamples.q: Calculate ΔH for C(s) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g) using ΔHc°: C = −393, H₂ = −286, CH₄ = −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
In a calorimetry experiment, 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl is mixed with 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Temperature rises by 6.8°C. Calculate ΔHneut.

mistakes: Using ΔHc° formula without reversing the sign for products in a Hess combustion cycle.
Forgetting the negative sign in ΔH = −q/n for calorimetry.
Using bond enthalpies for ionic or aqueous reactions — they only apply to gaseous covalent species.
tips: Label every arrow on a Hess cycle with the correct sign and value before arithmetic.
In bond enthalpy questions, always draw out the full structural formula to count bonds correctly.
q = mcΔT: m is the mass of the solution (usually the total volume in g), not the mass of the solute.

flashcards.q: What is the formula for calorimetry?
flashcards.a: q = mcΔT (m in g, c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, ΔT in °C or K)
The total enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken.

flashcards.q: How do you calculate ΔH from bond enthalpies?
flashcards.a: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed); breaking is +, forming is −.

flashcards.q: State the standard condition for enthalpy measurements.
flashcards.a: 298 K (25°C) and 100 kPa, with all substances in their standard states.

flashcards.q: What sign does ΔH have for an exothermic reaction?
flashcards.a: Negative (ΔH < 0) — energy is released to surroundings.

flashcards.q: Why are bond enthalpy calculations less accurate than Hess's law cycles?
flashcards.a: Mean bond enthalpies are averages across many compounds; Hess's law uses precise experimental values.

questions.q: ΔHf° for CO₂ is −394 kJ mol⁻¹. What does this mean?
opts: 1 mol CO₂ releases 394 kJ when burned
1 mol CO₂ forms from C(s)+O₂(g) releasing 394 kJ
1 mol CO releases 394 kJ when oxidised
questions.exp: Standard enthalpy of formation: 1 mol of product forms from elements in standard states, releasing 394 kJ.

questions.q: 50 g of water heats by 8°C. What is q?
ΔH for A→B = +50 kJ; ΔH for A→C = −30 kJ. What is ΔH for B→C?
Which statement about bond enthalpies is correct?
opts: Bond enthalpies are exact values for each molecule
Mean bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds
questions.exp: Mean bond enthalpies are averages — they give approximate, not exact, ΔH values.

questions.exp: Strong acid + strong base: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l); ΔH ≈ −57 kJ mol⁻¹.
